Case Vignette: Anjali

Anjali is a 25-year-old South Asian woman who works as a counselor at a community mental health center. She presents as articulate and composed, though her eyes frequently dart to the exit during our sessions. She begins by saying, “I know the textbook. I help people with this. But I can’t get out of my own head.”

The event happened eight months ago, on a Tuesday evening in late November. Anjali had just finished a late session with a client and was walking the three blocks to her car. She remembers the cold air on her face, the dim streetlights, the sound of her own footsteps. A police cruiser pulled up beside her. Two officers got out. She was holding her phone, checking her schedule for the next day. They asked where she was going. She told them. They asked why she was in this neighborhood. She said she worked here. They asked for her ID. She handed it over. One officer said something she cannot quite recall, something about "suspicious activity." The other officer pushed her against the wall of a laundromat. She felt the cold brick through her jacket, the pressure of a knee in her lower back. She remembers thinking, I’m a counselor. I help people. I’m not a threat. She did not resist. She said, “I’m sorry. I’m sorry. I’m just going home.” They let her go after fifteen minutes. No charges. No ticket. Just a warning to “be more careful.”

Since that night, Anjali’s world has shrunk. She no longer walks anywhere after dark. She drives to work even though it is only a mile from her apartment, and she circles the block three times to find a spot directly under a streetlight. She has stopped going to the grocery store after 5 p.m. She avoids eye contact with anyone in uniform—police, security guards, even the parking enforcement officer. Her heart pounds when she hears a siren, even from blocks away. She has changed her route to work three times, always choosing the one with the most traffic, the most witnesses.

At work, Anjali is still competent, but she is different. She finds herself scanning the waiting room before each session. She has started wearing muted colors—gray, brown, black—as if to disappear. She flinches when a client raises their voice in anger or distress, even when it is directed at someone else. She has stopped taking evening clients. She tells her supervisor it is for "self-care," but really, she cannot bear the thought of being outside after dark.

She has trouble sleeping. She lies awake replaying the moment of the push, the cold brick, the knee. Sometimes she dreams of it, but in the dream, the officers are not white men; they are her clients, her colleagues, her father. She wakes up drenched in sweat, her jaw clenched, her hands balled into fists. She has started drinking one glass of wine before bed to quiet her mind, then two.

She is irritable with her mother, who calls every evening to ask if she has eaten. She snaps at her roommate for leaving the back door unlocked. She has stopped going to the weekly potluck with her coworkers because the crowded room feels like a trap. She tells herself she is just being careful, that this is what the world is like, that she needs to protect herself.

But she also feels a deep, quiet shame. She is a counselor. She knows the statistics. She knows that Black and Brown people are disproportionately targeted by police. She knows that her own South Asian identity did not protect her that night, but she also knows that many others have it worse. She tells herself she should be stronger, that she should be able to move past this. She tells herself that she is overreacting. She tells herself that she is failing her clients by being so fragile.

Yet, she cannot stop the hypervigilance. She cannot stop the startle response. She cannot stop the feeling that she is always, always about to be caught.
